Certain infectious, congenital, and hereditary eye diseases may be manifest at birth, and since they create a risk to vision if undetected, a screening in the newborn is justified. Infants who have abnormalities detected as well as infants with risk factors such as systemic diseases or a family history of certain conditions should be referred for a comprehensive eye examination by an ophthalmologist. Children should receive a series of age-appropriate screenings during primary health care visits throughout childhood because different childhood eye problems may be detected at each visit and new problems can arise during childhood. Because amblyopia is estimated to occur at a rate of two to three percent in this age group and may lead to functional blindness if undetected, any child with an abnormal subjective visual acuity assessment or one who has not been successfully tested by age 4 should be referred for a comprehensive eye examination by an ophthalmologist. The major abnormality among school-age children is the unrecognized development and progression of myopic refractive error, and individuals in this age group should be examined. Myopia can develop in individuals in their 20s, and it can progress in those whose refractive error did not stabilize in the teenage years. In the young adult the rate of development of other significant eye disease is low, but it increases steadily after the age of 40. Evaluation: Before the onset of presbyopia (at approximately age 40), the majority of American adults experience no changing refractive error or significant ocular disease and routine eye examinations are not indicated. Adults with no signs or risk factors for eye disease should receive a baseline comprehensive eye evaluation at age 40. For asymptomatic individuals or individuals without risk factors who are 40 to 54 years old and who have had a comprehensive eye examination, the recommended interval for evaluations is 2 to 4 years. For individuals aged 55 to 64 years old, the recommended interval for evaluations is 1 to 3 years. For individuals 65 years old or older, the American Academy of Ophthalmology recommends an examination every 1 to 2 years, even in the absence of symptoms. fetched_contents.text: Comprehensive eye exams Periodic eye and vision examinations are an important part of preventive healthcare. Many eye and vision problems have no obvious signs or symptoms, so you might not know a problem exists. Early diagnosis and treatment of eye and vision problems can help prevent vision loss. Each patient's signs and symptoms, along with your doctor of optometry's professional judgment, will determine what tests are conducted. A comprehensive adult eye and vision examination may include but is not limited to, the following tests. Patient history The doctor will ask about any eye or vision problems you are currently having and about your overall health. In addition, a patient history will include when your eye or vision symptoms began, medications you are taking, and any work-related or environmental conditions that may be affecting your vision. The doctor will also ask about any previous eye or health conditions you and your family members have experienced. Visual acuity Visual acuity measurements evaluate how clearly each eye is seeing. Reading charts are often used to measure visual acuity. As part of the testing, you will read letters on charts at a distance and near. The results of visual acuity testing are written as a fraction, such as 20/40. The top number in the fraction is the standard distance at which testing is done (20 feet). The bottom number is the smallest letter size you were able to read. A person with 20/40 visual acuity would have to get within 20 feet to see a letter that should be seen clearly at 40 feet. Normal distance visual acuity is 20/20. Preliminary tests A doctor of optometry may first want to look at specific aspects of the patient's visual function and eye health. Preliminary tests can include evaluations of depth perception, color vision, eye muscle movements, peripheral or side vision, and the way your pupils respond to light. Keratometry/topography These tests measure the curvature of the cornea (the clear outer surface of the eye) by focusing a circle of light on the cornea and measuring its reflection. This measurement is particularly critical in determining the proper fit for contact lenses. Refraction Refraction determines the lens power needed to compensate for any refractive error (nearsightedness, farsightedness or astigmatism). Using an instrument called a phoropter, the doctor places a series of lenses in front of your eyes. He or she then measures how these lenses focus light using a handheld lighted instrument called a retinoscope. The doctor may choose to use an instrument that automatically evaluates the focusing power of the eye. The lens power is then refined based on the patient's input on the lenses that give you the clearest vision. This testing can be done without eye drops to determine how the eyes respond under normal seeing conditions. However, a doctor of optometry will use eye drops with patients who can't respond verbally or when some of the eyes' focusing power may be hidden. The drops temporarily keep the eyes from changing focus during testing. Eye focusing, eye teaming, and eye movement testing To see a clear, single image, the eyes must effectively change focus, move and work in unison. An assessment of accommodation, ocular motility, and binocular vision determines how well your eyes focus, move and work together. This testing will look for problems that keep eyes from focusing effectively or make using both eyes together difficult. Eye health evaluation A wide variety of microscopes, lense, and digital technology will be used to assess the health of all the structures of the eye and the surrounding tissues. Dilating eye drops are often used to temporarily widen the pupil for better views of the structures inside the eye. In addition to measuring the pressure inside of the eye, this also is part of the eye exam where a doctor of optometry can detect otherwise unknown eye and systemic diseases. Supplemental testing Additional testing may be needed based on the results of the previous tests to confirm or rule out possible problems, to clarify uncertain findings, or to provide a more in-depth assessment. At the completion of the examination, the doctor will assess and evaluate the results of the testing to determine a diagnosis and develop a treatment plan. He or she will discuss with you the nature of any visual or eye health problems found and explain available treatment options. In some cases, referral for consultation with, or treatment by, another doctor of optometry or other healthcare provider may be indicated. If you have questions about any diagnosed eye or vision conditions, or treatment recommendations, don't hesitate to ask your doctor for additional information or explanation. fetched_contents.text: Evaluating Health Information: MedlinePlus On this page Learn More * Related Issues * Specifics See, Play and Learn * Videos and Tutorials Research * Journal Articles Summary Why do I need to evaluate health information? Health information is easy to find. But finding reliable health information takes a little effort. Some of the health information you get from newspapers, magazines, books, TV, the Internet, and social media is up to date and trustworthy. But some is not. That's why it's important to evaluate health information for yourself. But how can you tell the good from the bad? There are two key steps: * Ask questions before you trust what you read or hear. * Discuss the information you find with your health care provider before you rely on it. You may have found good information, but your provider can tell you whether it's good for you. How can I evaluate health information on the Internet? Asking a few questions will help you decide if you can trust a website. You can usually find most of the answers on the site's "About Us" page. If you can't find information about who runs the website, the site may not be trustworthy, and their health information may be unreliable. Some questions to ask are: * Who runs the site? Can you trust them to provide balanced, accurate information? Trustworthy sites provide a way to contact the owners with questions or feedback. In general, you'll find good health information on websites run by: * Federal government agencies. * Medical schools. * Large professional or nonprofit organizations. For example, the American College of Cardiology (a professional organization) and the American Heart Association (a nonprofit) and are both reliable sources of information on heart health. * What's the purpose of the site? Is it to: * Inform the public? * Sell products or services? * Promote the opinions of a person or group? A trustworthy website has one goal: To give you good information. * Who pays for the site? * If the site is funded by ads, they should be clearly marked as advertisements. Watch out for ads designed to look like neutral health information. * If a business pays for the site, the health information may favor that business and its products. * Is the health information high quality? Good health information doesn't promote one treatment over another. It gives you balanced facts based on research. So, beware of dramatic writing, promises of cures, and claims that sound too good to be true. Those could be signs of a health fraud scam. To evaluate the quality of a website's information, ask: * How is the information selected and reviewed to make sure it's accurate? Check the "About Us" page to see if the site has: * An editorial board of health experts * A content review process * A selection policy for content * Information about their writers' qualifications, which may be listed at the bottom of the articles * Where does the information come from? The content pages should have links or references to the sources of the information. * Is the information up to date? Content pages should include dates when the information was written, reviewed, or updated. * How does the website use your personal information? Look for a privacy policy section to see how your personal information will be used. Don't share information about yourself unless you're comfortable with any risks involved. When you find a website that seems to be trustworthy, don't stop there. Look to see if other reliable sites have similar health information. How can I evaluate health information on social media? A social media post may come from someone you know, but that doesn't guarantee it's good information. Many of the questions you use to evaluate a website also work for social media too. Ask where the information comes from, why it exists, and if anyone is funding it. If you're not sure whether the information you see on social media is trustworthy, don"t share it with others. How can I evaluate health stories in the news? Some news stories about medical research may not include all the facts you need to know. Ask these questions: * Does the story say whether the research involved people or animals? * If it was people, how many people were in the study and who were they? * How long was the study? * What type of study was it? * Who paid for the research? If you learn a few tips for understanding medical research, you'll be able to decide if a news story may apply to your health. Then you can discuss the information with your provider. How can I evaluate health information in books? To evaluate health information in books, ask: * How old is the book? * Is the author an expert on the subject? * Does the book offer different points of view or just those of the author? * Has the book been reviewed by other experts? * Does the book list the sources of the content? After you evaluate health information, talk with your provider before using it to make decisions that may affect your health. Evidence-based recommendation for eye exams every 1-2 years

The strongest evidence supports age-based intervals rather than a one-size-fits-all recommendation. The American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO) guideline states that adults with no symptoms and at low risk should receive a baseline comprehensive eye evaluation at age 40, then follow a periodic schedule designed to detect ocular disease [N1-F1]. For asymptomatic individuals or those without risk factors, the AAO recommends evaluations every 2 to 4 years for those aged 40 to 54, every 1 to 3 years for those aged 55 to 64, and every 1 to 2 years for those 65 years or older, even in the absence of symptoms [N1-F1]. AAO also notes that young adults at higher risk for certain diseases, such as African-Americans at higher risk for glaucoma, may be considered every 2 to 4 years for those under age 40, every 1 to 3 years for 40 to 54 years, and every 1 to 2 years for 55 to 64 years [N1-F1].

Other sources similarly support 1- to 2-year intervals for some adult groups. The AOA patient-facing page states that patients who have undergone refractive surgery (LASIK, PRK, SMILE) should still have an eye exam every 1-2 years for monitoring of overall ocular health [N3-R1]. Aetna’s patient guide notes that doctors recommend regular eye exams based on age or medical history even when there are no symptoms or vision problems [N2-R3]. The Facebook post “When Should You Schedule an Eye Exam?” says adults can get by with an eye exam every 1-2 years, even if they feel their vision is fine [N1-R4]. Taken together, these sources support 1- to 2-year exams as a reasonable interval for many adults, especially those without symptoms, but only as part of a more nuanced age- and risk-based recommendation [N1-F1][N3-R1][N1-R4].

Conditions under which a longer interval may be reasonable

A longer interval may be reasonable for low-risk individuals who have no symptoms and no known risk factors. The AAO guideline says adults who have no signs or risk factors for eye disease should receive a baseline comprehensive eye evaluation at age 40, and then follow a periodic schedule [N1-F1]. It also says that individuals who have no symptoms and who are at low risk should receive an initial comprehensive eye examination and then follow a schedule designed to detect ocular disease [N1-F1]. For asymptomatic individuals or those without risk factors, the AAO recommends 2- to 4-year intervals for 40- to 54-year-olds and 1- to 3-year intervals for 55- to 64-year-olds [N1-F1]. That means the longer interval is not universal, but rather tied to low risk and absence of symptoms.

Evidence gaps or limitations

The evidence base is not perfect. The AAO guideline is the most authoritative here, but it is a clinical statement rather than a randomized controlled trial, so its recommendations are based on systematic review and clinical judgment rather than direct proof of outcomes [N1-R3]. The search results also include more general sources and patient-facing pages, which can be helpful but are less direct evidence than the AAO guideline [N2-R1][N3-R1]. A key limitation is that the literature on eye exam frequency is often age- and risk-specific, so a single “every 1-2 years” recommendation can be misleading if applied to someone who is younger, lower-risk, or has a different medical history [N1-F1]. The provided evidence does not include a large randomized trial comparing 1-2-year exams versus less frequent exams, so the recommendation remains best practice rather than proven by controlled study [N1-F1].

Why an eye exam may still be needed even if vision appears fine

Conditions that can cause asymptomatic vision changes or eye disease

The evidence shows that many eye diseases can develop without early symptoms. The AAO page explains that eye exams are not just about vision; they are about health, and that many eye diseases show no early symptoms [N2-R1]. The same source states that regular exams help detect problems before vision is affected [N2-R1]. The “20 Surprising Health Problems an Eye Exam Can Catch” page notes that eye exams can detect diabetes, autoimmune diseases, high blood pressure, and other systemic conditions [N2-R1]. The CDC diabetes page adds that people with diabetes are at higher risk of vision loss and eye diseases such as retinopathy, glaucoma, and cataracts [N4-R3]. Another source says annual dilated eye exams are the most effective way to detect diabetic eye disease early and begin treatment before serious vision loss occurs [N4-R5]. Together, these sources indicate that eye exams can identify diseases and conditions that do not cause obvious vision changes at first.

Early detection benefits health outcomes

Early detection is important because it allows treatment to begin before serious vision loss or complications occur. The AAO notes that many eye and vision problems have no obvious signs or symptoms, so early diagnosis and treatment can help prevent vision loss [N3-F2]. The CDC diabetes page says that people with diabetes are at higher risk of vision loss and eye diseases, reinforcing that early intervention can reduce that risk [N4-R3]. The “20 Surprising Health Problems an Eye Exam Can Catch” page similarly emphasizes that exams can detect problems before vision is affected [N2-R1]. In practical terms, early detection may help preserve vision and prevent downstream complications, especially for conditions like diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, and hypertension-related eye disease [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R5].

What patients should expect during a routine eye exam

A routine eye exam is not limited to reading an eye chart. The AOA patient-facing page explains that a comprehensive adult eye and vision examination may include visual acuity testing, preliminary tests of depth perception, color vision, eye muscle movements, peripheral vision, and pupil response to light, as well as keratometry/topography, refraction, and eye focusing, eye teaming, and eye movement testing [N3-F2]. It also notes that a wide variety of microscopes, lenses, and digital technology are used to assess the health of all eye structures and surrounding tissues, and that dilating drops may be used to get a better view inside the eye [N3-F2]. The same source says that the doctor will ask about symptoms, medications, work-related or environmental conditions, and family history, and that the exam may include supplemental testing if needed [N3-F2]. Overall, a routine eye exam is a thorough assessment of both vision and ocular health, not just a quick check for blurry vision [N3-F2].

How to find trustworthy health websites or professional organizations

The evidence points to several trustworthy sources. The National Institutes of Health website is recommended as a good place to start for reliable health information [N5-R1]. MedlinePlus is also cited as a source for evaluating health information [N5-R2][N5-F3]. The AAO and Aetna pages are directly relevant here as well, because they are professional or insurance-based sources that provide patient-facing guidance on eye exams [N3-R1][N2-R3]. The search results also mention federal government agencies, medical schools, and large professional or nonprofit organizations as reliable sources [N5-F3]. In practical terms, patients should prioritize sites run by government agencies, academic institutions, major medical associations, and established health organizations rather than random websites or commercial pages [N5-F3].

What questions to ask when evaluating a source

The evidence gives a clear framework for evaluating a source. MedlinePlus recommends asking who runs the site, the purpose of the site, who pays for the site, and whether the health information is high quality [N5-F3]. It also suggests checking whether the site has an editorial board, a content review process, a selection policy for content, and information about writers’ qualifications [N5-F3]. The same source advises looking for dates on the content pages to see whether the information is up to date [N5-F3]. Another source says to ask whether the information is recent and/or regularly reviewed and updated, and what the purpose of the site is [N6-R4]. The “How to Find Reliable Health Information Online” guide adds that .gov, .edu, and .org sites are often reliable and advises checking domain names [N6-R3]. In short, patients should ask: who runs the site, what the site’s purpose is, who pays for it, whether the information is reviewed and up to date, and whether the source is backed by credible experts [N5-F3][N6-R3][N6-R4].

How to locate a doctor or clinic for an eye exam

The evidence does not provide a detailed directory of clinics, but it does give a practical path. The patient-facing AAO page states that patients who have undergone refractive surgery should still have an eye exam every 1-2 years for monitoring of overall ocular health [N3-R1]. The Aetna guide notes that doctors recommend regular eye exams based on age or medical history [N2-R3]. The CDC eye exam page says that the exam may be done by an ophthalmologist and may involve referral for consultation with another provider if needed [N3-F2]. In practice, a patient should contact an ophthalmologist’s office or an optometry clinic directly and ask about the recommended frequency for their situation [N3-F2]. Because the evidence here is mainly guidance rather than a clinic directory, the most useful next step is to reach out to a licensed eye care provider and ask for their recommendation based on age, medical history, and risk factors [N3-F2].

How to verify a medical recommendation and avoid unreliable sources

Which websites and organizations are most trustworthy

The most trustworthy sources cited in the evidence are federal government agencies, medical schools, large professional or nonprofit organizations, and established health organizations [N5-F3]. Specifically, MedlinePlus, the National Institutes of Health, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention are named as reliable sources [N5-R1][N5-R2]. The AAO and Aetna pages are also trustworthy because they are professional or insurance-based sources with patient-facing guidance [N3-R1][N2-R3]. The search results also indicate that .gov, .edu, and .org sites are often reliable [N6-R3]. In practice, patients should prioritize these kinds of sites over random commercial or unaffiliated websites [N5-F3][N6-R3].

How to cross-check claims with multiple reliable sources

The evidence emphasizes cross-checking with multiple reliable sources. MedlinePlus advises looking to see if other reliable sites have similar health information [N5-F3]. The “How to Find Reliable Health Information Online” guide says to do a web search to check if other reputable sources confirm the health claim [N5-R5]. The same logic applies here: if a claim says an eye exam every 1-2 years is recommended, the patient should check that claim against the AAO guideline, the AOA page, Aetna’s patient guide, and other authoritative sources rather than relying on one source alone [N1-F1][N3-R1][N2-R3]. The evidence also supports using government and academic sources together because they are more likely to be consistent with the best scientific evidence [N5-R1][N5-R2].

How to recognize red flags in health claims

The evidence gives several red flags to watch for. MedlinePlus warns against dramatic writing, promises of cures, and claims that sound too good to be true [N5-F3]. It also notes that if a site is funded by ads, those should be clearly marked as advertisements, and that business-funded sites may favor that business and its products [N5-F3]. The “How to Find Reliable Health Information Online” guide says to avoid sites whose purpose is to sell products or services rather than inform the public [N6-R3]. The same source advises being cautious if the information is not up to date or if the site does not provide contact information, an editorial board, or clear references [N5-F3]. In short, red flags include overly dramatic language, unclear funding, a commercial purpose, missing credentials, and lack of up-to-date review [N5-F3][N6-R3].

## Short answer

If you want to know whether an eye exam every 1–2 years is recommended even if your vision seems fine, the best approach is to start with **age-based guidelines** and then check **trusted sources** for your situation. The strongest evidence supports that many adults may need exams every 1–2 years, especially as they age or if they have no symptoms and low risk [N1-F1][N3-R1][N1-R4]. But the recommendation is not the same for everyone, so you should also verify the claim with **multiple reliable sources** and ask a licensed eye care provider what is right for you [N5-F3][N6-R3].

## 1. What the evidence says about 1–2-year eye exams

The strongest evidence comes from the **American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO)** guideline. It says adults who have no symptoms and are at low risk should receive a baseline comprehensive eye evaluation at age 40 and then follow a periodic schedule designed to detect ocular disease [N1-F1]. For asymptomatic individuals or those without risk factors, it recommends:

- **40–54 years old:** every 2 to 4 years  
- **55–64 years old:** every 1 to 3 years  
- **65 years or older:** every 1 to 2 years, even in the absence of symptoms [N1-F1]

Other sources support a 1–2-year interval for some adult groups. The **American Optometric Association (AOA)** patient-facing page says people who have had refractive surgery should still have an eye exam every 1–2 years for monitoring of overall ocular health [N3-R1]. Aetna also states that doctors recommend regular eye exams based on age or medical history even when there are no symptoms or vision problems [N2-R3]. A Facebook post similarly says adults can get by with an eye exam every 1–2 years, even if they feel their vision is fine [N1-R4].

So, the short answer is: **yes, many adults can reasonably get an eye exam every 1–2 years if they are asymptomatic and low-risk**, but the exact interval depends on age, risk factors, and medical history [N1-F1][N3-R1][N1-R4].

## 2. Why an eye exam may still be needed even if vision seems fine

Even if your vision appears fine, an eye exam can detect problems before they cause symptoms. The evidence shows that many eye diseases can develop **without early symptoms** [N2-R1]. For example:

- **Diabetic eye disease** can be detected early with annual dilated eye exams, which help begin treatment before serious vision loss occurs [N4-R5]
- **Glaucoma** is often called the “silent thief of sight” because it can progress without noticeable symptoms [N4-R1]
- **High blood pressure and other systemic conditions** can also be detected through eye exams [N4-R1][N4-R2]
- **Diabetes** increases the risk of retinopathy, glaucoma, and cataracts, so eye exams are especially important for people with diabetes [N4-R3]

This means an eye exam is not just about blurry vision. It can catch conditions that affect your overall health and can change over time [N2-R1][N4-R3][N4-R5].

## 3. What happens during a routine eye exam

A routine eye exam is more than just reading an eye chart. The AOA patient guide explains that a comprehensive adult eye and vision examination may include:

- **Visual acuity testing**  
- **Preliminary tests** of depth perception, color vision, eye muscle movements, peripheral vision, and pupil response to light  
- **Keratometry/topography**, **refraction**, and **eye focusing, eye teaming, and eye movement testing**  
- **Eye health evaluation** using microscopes, lenses, and digital technology, often with **dilating drops** to get a better view inside the eye [N3-F2]

The doctor will also ask about symptoms, medications, work-related or environmental conditions, and family history, and may do **supplemental testing** if needed [N3-F2]. In short, a routine exam is a **thorough assessment of both vision and ocular health** [N3-F2].

## 4. Practical steps to check the recommendation for yourself

If you want to verify the recommendation on your own, follow these steps:

### a) Use trusted health websites and professional organizations

The evidence points to several reliable sources:

- **Federal government agencies**  
- **Medical schools**  
- **Large professional or nonprofit organizations**  
- **Established health organizations** [N5-F3]

In practice, you should prioritize sites run by **.gov, .edu, or .org** institutions, and especially the **AAO**, **AOA**, and **CDC** pages, which are directly relevant to eye exams [N5-F3][N5-R1][N5-R2][N3-R1][N3-F2].

### b) Ask these questions when evaluating a source

MedlinePlus recommends asking:

- **Who runs the site?** Can you trust them to provide balanced, accurate information?  
- **What is the purpose of the site?** Is it to inform the public, sell products, or promote opinions?  
- **Who pays for the site?**  
- **Is the health information high quality?**  
- **How is the information selected and reviewed to make sure it is accurate?**  
- **Where does the information come from?**  
- **Is the information up to date?** [N5-F3]

The “How to Find Reliable Health Information Online” guide also says to ask whether the information is recent and/or regularly reviewed and updated, and whether the site’s purpose is clear [N6-R4].

### c) Cross-check claims with multiple reliable sources

The evidence supports cross-checking claims with multiple sources. MedlinePlus says to check if other reliable sites have similar health information, and the “How to Find Reliable Health Information Online” guide advises doing a web search to confirm the claim with other reputable sources [N5-F3][N5-R5]. That means if you find a claim that 1–2-year exams are recommended, you should check it against the AAO guideline, the AOA page, Aetna’s patient guide, and other authoritative sources [N1-F1][N3-R1][N2-R3].

### d) Locate a doctor or clinic for an eye exam

The evidence does not provide a clinic directory, but it does show that the right next step is to contact an **ophthalmologist’s office or an optometry clinic** and ask about the recommended frequency for your situation [N3-F2]. Because the evidence is mainly guidance, the most useful next step is to reach out to a licensed eye care provider and ask them what is right for your age, medical history, and risk factors [N3-F2].

## 5. How to avoid unreliable sources

To avoid unreliable sources, watch for these red flags:

- **Dramatic writing, promises of cures, or claims that sound too good to be true** [N5-F3]
- **Ads that are not clearly marked** or business-funded sites that may favor a product or service [N5-F3]
- **Sites whose purpose is to sell products or services rather than inform the public** [N6-R3]
- **Lack of contact information, editorial board, or clear references** [N5-F3]
- **Outdated information or no update dates** [N5-F3]

If a site makes you uncomfortable, don’t share it with others and consider checking the claim against multiple reliable sources [N5-F3].

## 6. Bottom line

If you want to know whether an eye exam every 1–2 years is recommended even if your vision seems fine, here’s what you should do:

1. **Start with age-based guidelines** and look for sources like the AAO and AOA [N1-F1][N3-R1].  
2. **Check trusted websites** such as government pages, medical schools, and large professional organizations [N5-F3][N5-R1].  
3. **Ask questions about the source** to see whether it is reliable and up to date [N5-F3][N6-R4].  
4. **Cross-check the claim** against multiple authoritative sources [N5-F3][N5-R5].  
5. **Talk to an eye care provider** to get a personalized recommendation [N3-F2].  
6. **Be cautious of red flags** such as overly dramatic claims, unclear funding, or commercial purposes [N5-F3][N6-R3].

In short: **yes, many adults can reasonably get an eye exam every 1–2 years even if their vision seems fine**, but the exact interval depends on your age, risk factors, and medical history [N1-F1][N3-R1][N1-R4].

Evidence-based recommendation for eye exams every 1-2 years

The strongest evidence supports age-based intervals rather than a one-size-fits-all recommendation. The American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO) guideline states that adults with no symptoms and at low risk should receive a baseline comprehensive eye evaluation at age 40, then follow a periodic schedule designed to detect ocular disease [N1-F1]. For asymptomatic individuals or those without risk factors, the AAO recommends evaluations every 2 to 4 years for those aged 40 to 54, every 1 to 3 years for those aged 55 to 64, and every 1 to 2 years for those 65 years or older, even in the absence of symptoms [N1-F1]. AAO also notes that young adults at higher risk for certain diseases, such as African-Americans at higher risk for glaucoma, may be considered every 2 to 4 years for those under age 40, every 1 to 3 years for 40 to 54 years, and every 1 to 2 years for 55 to 64 years [N1-F1].

Other sources similarly support 1- to 2-year intervals for some adult groups. The AOA patient-facing page states that patients who have undergone refractive surgery (LASIK, PRK, SMILE) should still have an eye exam every 1-2 years for monitoring of overall ocular health [N3-R1]. Aetna’s patient guide notes that doctors recommend regular eye exams based on age or medical history even when there are no symptoms or vision problems [N2-R3]. The Facebook post “When Should You Schedule an Eye Exam?” says adults can get by with an eye exam every 1-2 years, even if they feel their vision is fine [N1-R4]. Taken together, these sources support 1- to 2-year exams as a reasonable interval for many adults, especially those without symptoms, but only as part of a more nuanced age- and risk-based recommendation [N1-F1][N3-R1][N1-R4].

Conditions under which a longer interval may be reasonable

A longer interval may be reasonable for low-risk individuals who have no symptoms and no known risk factors. The AAO guideline says adults who have no signs or risk factors for eye disease should receive a baseline comprehensive eye evaluation at age 40, and then follow a periodic schedule [N1-F1]. It also says that individuals who have no symptoms and who are at low risk should receive an initial comprehensive eye examination and then follow a schedule designed to detect ocular disease [N1-F1]. For asymptomatic individuals or those without risk factors, the AAO recommends 2- to 4-year intervals for 40- to 54-year-olds and 1- to 3-year intervals for 55- to 64-year-olds [N1-F1]. That means the longer interval is not universal, but rather tied to low risk and absence of symptoms.

Evidence gaps or limitations

The evidence base is not perfect. The AAO guideline is the most authoritative here, but it is a clinical statement rather than a randomized controlled trial, so its recommendations are based on systematic review and clinical judgment rather than direct proof of outcomes [N1-R3]. The search results also include more general sources and patient-facing pages, which can be helpful but are less direct evidence than the AAO guideline [N2-R1][N3-R1]. A key limitation is that the literature on eye exam frequency is often age- and risk-specific, so a single “every 1-2 years” recommendation can be misleading if applied to someone who is younger, lower-risk, or has a different medical history [N1-F1]. The provided evidence does not include a large randomized trial comparing 1-2-year exams versus less frequent exams, so the recommendation remains best practice rather than proven by controlled study [N1-F1].

Why an eye exam may still be needed even if vision appears fine

Conditions that can cause asymptomatic vision changes or eye disease

The evidence shows that many eye diseases can develop without early symptoms. The AAO page explains that eye exams are not just about vision; they are about health, and that many eye diseases show no early symptoms [N2-R1]. The same source states that regular exams help detect problems before vision is affected [N2-R1]. The “20 Surprising Health Problems an Eye Exam Can Catch” page notes that eye exams can detect diabetes, autoimmune diseases, high blood pressure, and other systemic conditions [N2-R1]. The CDC diabetes page adds that people with diabetes are at higher risk of vision loss and eye diseases such as retinopathy, glaucoma, and cataracts [N4-R3]. Another source says annual dilated eye exams are the most effective way to detect diabetic eye disease early and begin treatment before serious vision loss occurs [N4-R5]. Together, these sources indicate that eye exams can identify diseases and conditions that do not cause obvious vision changes at first.

Early detection benefits health outcomes

Early detection is important because it allows treatment to begin before serious vision loss or complications occur. The AAO notes that many eye and vision problems have no obvious signs or symptoms, so early diagnosis and treatment can help prevent vision loss [N3-F2]. The CDC diabetes page says that people with diabetes are at higher risk of vision loss and eye diseases, reinforcing that early intervention can reduce that risk [N4-R3]. The “20 Surprising Health Problems an Eye Exam Can Catch” page similarly emphasizes that exams can detect problems before vision is affected [N2-R1]. In practical terms, early detection may help preserve vision and prevent downstream complications, especially for conditions like diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, and hypertension-related eye disease [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R5].

What patients should expect during a routine eye exam

A routine eye exam is not limited to reading an eye chart. The AOA patient-facing page explains that a comprehensive adult eye and vision examination may include visual acuity testing, preliminary tests of depth perception, color vision, eye muscle movements, peripheral vision, and pupil response to light, as well as keratometry/topography, refraction, and eye focusing, eye teaming, and eye movement testing [N3-F2]. It also notes that a wide variety of microscopes, lenses, and digital technology are used to assess the health of all eye structures and surrounding tissues, and that dilating drops may be used to get a better view inside the eye [N3-F2]. The same source says that the doctor will ask about symptoms, medications, work-related or environmental conditions, and family history, and that the exam may include supplemental testing if needed [N3-F2]. Overall, a routine eye exam is a thorough assessment of both vision and ocular health, not just a quick check for blurry vision [N3-F2].

## Short answer

The strongest evidence supports that many adults may need exams every 1–2 years, especially as they age or if they have no symptoms and low risk [N1-F1][N3-R1][N1-R4]. But the recommendation is not the same for everyone, so you should also verify the claim with **multiple reliable sources** and ask a licensed eye care provider what is right for you [N5-F3][N6-R3].

## 1. What the evidence says about 1–2-year eye exams

The strongest evidence comes from the **American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO)** guideline. It says adults who have no symptoms and are at low risk should receive a baseline comprehensive eye evaluation at age 40 and then follow a periodic schedule designed to detect ocular disease [N1-F1]. For asymptomatic individuals or those without risk factors, it recommends:

- **40–54 years old:** every 2 to 4 years  
- **55–64 years old:** every 1 to 3 years  
- **65 years or older:** every 1 to 2 years, even in the absence of symptoms [N1-F1]

Other sources support a 1–2-year interval for some adult groups. The **American Optometric Association (AOA)** patient-facing page says people who have had refractive surgery should still have an eye exam every 1–2 years for monitoring of overall ocular health [N3-R1]. Aetna also states that doctors recommend regular eye exams based on age or medical history even when there are no symptoms or vision problems [N2-R3]. A Facebook post similarly says adults can get by with an eye exam every 1–2 years, even if they feel their vision is fine [N1-R4].

So, the short answer is: **yes, many adults can reasonably get an eye exam every 1–2 years if they are asymptomatic and low-risk**, but the exact interval depends on age, risk factors, and medical history [N1-F1][N3-R1][N1-R4].

## 2. Why an eye exam may still be needed even if vision seems fine

Even if your vision appears fine, an eye exam can detect problems before they cause symptoms. The evidence shows that many eye diseases can develop **without early symptoms** [N2-R1]. For example:

- **Diabetic eye disease** can be detected early with annual dilated eye exams, which help begin treatment before serious vision loss occurs [N4-R5]
- **Glaucoma** is often called the “silent thief of sight” because it can progress without noticeable symptoms [N4-R1]
- **High blood pressure and other systemic conditions** can also be detected through eye exams [N4-R1][N4-R2]
- **Diabetes** increases the risk of retinopathy, glaucoma, and cataracts, so eye exams are especially important for people with diabetes [N4-R3]

This means an eye exam is not just about blurry vision. It can catch conditions that affect your overall health and can change over time [N2-R1][N4-R3][N4-R5].

## 3. What happens during a routine eye exam

A routine eye exam is more than just reading an eye chart. The AOA patient guide explains that a comprehensive adult eye and vision examination may include:

- **Visual acuity testing**  
- **Preliminary tests** of depth perception, color vision, eye muscle movements, peripheral vision, and pupil response to light  
- **Keratometry/topography**, **refraction**, and **eye focusing, eye teaming, and eye movement testing**  
- **Eye health evaluation** using microscopes, lenses, and digital technology, often with **dilating drops** to get a better view inside the eye [N3-F2]

The doctor will also ask about symptoms, medications, work-related or environmental conditions, and family history, and may do **supplemental testing** if needed [N3-F2]. In short, a routine exam is a **thorough assessment of both vision and ocular health** [N3-F2].

### a) Use trusted health websites and professional organizations

The evidence points to several reliable sources:

- **Federal government agencies**  
- **Medical schools**  
- **Large professional or nonprofit organizations**  
- **Established health organizations** [N5-F3]

In practice, you should prioritize sites run by **.gov, .edu, or .org** institutions, and especially the **AAO**, **AOA**, and **CDC** pages, which are directly relevant to eye exams [N5-F3][N5-R1][N5-R2][N3-R1][N3-F2].

### b) Ask these questions when evaluating a source

MedlinePlus recommends asking:

- **Who runs the site?** Can you trust them to provide balanced, accurate information?  
- **What is the purpose of the site?** Is it to inform the public, sell products, or promote opinions?  
- **Who pays for the site?**  
- **Is the health information high quality?**  
- **How is the information selected and reviewed to make sure it is accurate?**  
- **Where does the information come from?**  
- **Is the information up to date?** [N5-F3]

The “How to Find Reliable Health Information Online” guide also says to ask whether the information is recent and/or regularly reviewed and updated, and whether the site’s purpose is clear [N6-R4].

### c) Cross-check claims with multiple reliable sources

The evidence supports cross-checking claims with multiple sources. MedlinePlus says to check if other reliable sites have similar health information, and the “How to Find Reliable Health Information Online” guide advises doing a web search to confirm the claim with other reputable sources [N5-F3][N5-R5]. That means if you find a claim that 1–2-year exams are recommended, you should check it against the AAO guideline, the AOA page, Aetna’s patient guide, and other authoritative sources [N1-F1][N3-R1][N2-R3].

Because the evidence is mainly guidance, the most useful next step is to reach out to a licensed eye care provider and ask them what is right for your age, medical history, and risk factors [N3-F2].

To avoid unreliable sources, watch for these red flags:

- **Dramatic writing, promises of cures, or claims that sound too good to be true** [N5-F3]
- **Ads that are not clearly marked** or business-funded sites that may favor a product or service [N5-F3]

- **Lack of contact information, editorial board, or clear references** [N5-F3]
- **Outdated information or no update dates** [N5-F3]

If a site makes you uncomfortable, don’t share it with others and consider checking the claim against multiple reliable sources [N5-F3].

## 6. Bottom line

If you want to know whether an eye exam every 1–2 years is recommended even if your vision seems fine, here’s what you should do:

1. **Start with age-based guidelines** and look for sources like the AAO and AOA [N1-F1][N3-R1].  
2. **Check trusted websites** such as government pages, medical schools, and large professional organizations [N5-F3][N5-R1].  
3. **Ask questions about the source** to see whether it is reliable and up to date [N5-F3][N6-R4].  
4. **Cross-check the claim** against multiple authoritative sources [N5-F3][N5-R5].  
5. **Talk to an eye care provider** to get a personalized recommendation [N3-F2].  
6. **Be cautious of red flags** such as overly dramatic claims, unclear funding, or commercial purposes [N5-F3][N6-R3].

In short: **yes, many adults can reasonably get an eye exam every 1–2 years even if their vision seems fine**, but the exact interval depends on your age, risk factors, and medical history [N1-F1][N3-R1][N1-R4].
